cardiomyopathy.short: A disease of the heart muscle itself (not the valves or the arteries) that changes its size, thickness or stiffness, or makes its rhythm unstable. Some kinds are inherited.

hcm.short: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: an inherited disease in which the heart wall, often the wall between the two ventricles, becomes abnormally thick without a matching bigger cavity.

arvc.short: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy: a mostly inherited disease in which heart muscle, mainly in the right ventricle, is replaced by scar and fat, which brings dangerous rhythm problems.

dcm.short: Dilated cardiomyopathy: the left ventricle, the main pumping chamber, is enlarged and pumps weakly. In an athlete it can be mistaken for a big, training-enlarged heart.

sudden-cardiac-death.short: Death from a sudden, unexpected stop of the heart's pumping, usually from a dangerous rhythm. In sport it happens during or soon after exercise.

grey-zone.short: The range of measurements where a healthy trained heart and a mild heart disease overlap, so one number cannot tell them apart.

t-wave-inversion.short: On an ECG, the T wave (the heart muscle resetting after each beat) normally points up. A T wave that points down in some leads needs a closer look in an athlete.

early-repolarisation.short: A common, usually harmless ECG pattern in which the signal after each beat lifts slightly before it settles. It is frequent in young, trained people.

av-block.short: An ECG finding in which the electrical signal takes slightly longer than usual to pass from the upper to the lower chambers. Every beat still gets through. Common in endurance athletes.

cpet.short: Cardiopulmonary exercise test: you exercise to exhaustion while a mask measures the gases you breathe and the heart is monitored. It gives VO₂peak and shows how efficiently you breathe.

atrial-fibrillation.short: A heart rhythm in which the two upper chambers (atria) quiver in a fast, disorganised way, so the pulse is irregular. It can come and go, and may bring palpitations, tiredness or no symptoms.

met-hours.short: A measure of activity dose: the activity's MET value times the hours done. One MET is resting energy use. Riding at 8 METs for 6 h is 48 MET-hours.

u-shaped-curve.short: A dose–response curve that falls and then rises: the outcome is best at a moderate dose and worse at both very low and very high doses. A J-shaped curve has a lower rise on the high side.

fibrosis.short: Scar-like tissue: stiff collagen laid down between muscle cells. In the atria it can disturb the spread of the electrical signal; in the ventricles it shows as patches on MRI.

cardiac-arrest.short: The heart suddenly stops pumping effectively: the person collapses, with no normal breathing and no pulse. Without treatment within minutes it ends in death.

case-fatality-rate.short: Of all the people who have an event (here, a cardiac arrest), the share who die.

athlete-year.short: One athlete followed for one year. A rate of 1 in 44,832 athlete-years means one event per 44,832 athletes each followed for a year.

wpw.short: WPW: an extra electrical connection between the upper and lower chambers of the heart that can allow dangerously fast rhythms. It shows on a resting ECG.

pre-participation-screening.short: Checking apparently healthy athletes before they play for hidden heart disease: questions about symptoms and family, a physical exam, and sometimes an ECG.

false-positive.short: A test result that signals disease in a person who does not have it. It leads to extra tests, worry and sometimes needless time out of sport.

number-needed-to-screen.short: How many people must be screened to find one true case. Smaller is better: 475 means about one true case for every 475 people screened.

cpr.short: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: pressing hard and fast on the centre of the chest, with or without rescue breaths, to keep blood moving until a shock or help arrives.

aed.short: Automated external defibrillator: a portable device that reads the heart rhythm and, if needed, gives an electric shock to restart a normal rhythm. Spoken steps guide a bystander.

extreme-exercise-hypothesis.short: The idea that exercise benefit follows a U-shape: very large amounts of long-term endurance training might harm the heart (calcium, scar, rhythm problems) and cancel part of the gain. Unproven.

coronary-artery-calcium.short: CAC: calcium deposits in the walls of the heart's own arteries, measured by a CT scan and reported as a score (0 means none). A high score predicts more heart attacks in the general population.

plaque.short: A build-up of fat, cells and calcium in an artery wall. Soft or mixed plaque can rupture; plaque that is only calcified is thought to be more stable.

atherosclerosis.short: The slow build-up of plaque in artery walls, which narrows them. If a plaque ruptures, a clot can block the artery and cause a heart attack.

late-gadolinium-enhancement.short: LGE: patches that light up on a contrast-enhanced heart MRI because the muscle there holds extra contrast, usually scar. Seen in some heart disease and in some healthy endurance athletes.
